body:
[https://prod.cdn.everyaction.com/images/van/NGP/NGP25/1/106220/images/PJM_Logo.png]
Will Congress Continue to be a Spectator?
The Iran war has been in a ceasefire since Wednesday with negotiations in Islamabad set for this weekend. There are reports that Iran has conducted drone strikes against our allies in Kuwait and Bahrain. I hope and pray it holds. But before we call this over, it's worth being honest about where things actually stand.
The global energy market has been disrupted in unprecedented ways by this war.
Before this war started, ships passed through the Strait of Hormuz freely — a waterway carrying roughly 20 percent of the world's oil supply. Over 100 vessels a day passed with no coordination required, no fees, and no permission needed from anyone.
That’s gone now.
Iran's foreign minister announced that passage through the Strait would now require "coordination with Iran's Armed Forces," with fees of up to $2 million per vessel — a structure Iran's parliament has already moved to codify into law. A waterway that Iran had no formal control over six weeks ago is now, functionally, a tollbooth the Islamic Republic operates. Iran is capping transit at 15 vessels a day and published routes that funnel traffic into Revolutionary Guard controlled water. Beyond those designated routes, at least a dozen underwater mines have been reported.
Iran entered this war under maximum sanctions and is now entering ceasefire negotiations demanding that the U.S. withdraw all military forces from the region (which is likely to be softened), accept continued uranium enrichment (which is likely to be softened), and pay reparations through ship transit fees.
That should tell you everything about how things have played out.
This outcome was foreseeable.
Earlier this week, the New York Times [https://www.nytimes.com/2026/04/07/us/politics/trump-iran-war.html] published what may be the most consequential piece of national security journalism since the Iraq War intelligence failures were laid bare. Jonathan Swan and Maggie Haberman, drawing on roughly 1,000 interviews for their forthcoming book on Trump’s second term, reconstructed the Situation Room meetings that took the United States into war with Iran. The details of how this war started are jarring and should concern every American, regardless of where they stand politically.
What the Times reporting makes impossible to ignore, is the process by which this specific decision was made.
On February 11, Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu came to the White House and delivered a four-part pitch: kill the Supreme Leader, destroy Iran's missile program, spark a popular uprising, and install a secular government. The CIA director reviewed the pitch overnight and the next morning, he used one word to describe the regime-change scenario: "farcical." Secretary Rubio agreed but supported the Iran War goal of degrading Iran’s military capability.
Despite pushback, President Trump decided to go through with it, partly thinking he could repeat a swift operation like the one he ordered in Venezuela - an overconfidence that has cost the lives of 13 American servicemembers and left 380 more wounded, as well as the thousands killed in that region, including civilians.
On Tuesday, I appeared on ABC News talking about the impact of this war. Watch here [https://www.instagram.com/p/DW7DaeRDZuk/] .
The War Tax
This war has been an expensive campaign the American people are paying for, and the math tells the story plainly.
Iran builds a drone for roughly $20,000. The United States fires a $2 million interceptor missile to knock it down, then does it again, and again, for weeks, against an adversary that sources components through Russia and China and rebuilds faster than we can replenish.
That's a 100-to-1 cost exchange sustained at scale against a country with an essentially unlimited supply of cheap materials and outside help filling the gaps.
The war has cost at least $12 billion so far and counting. Oil, which was around $70 a barrel before the war, shot past $100. Every American filling up their gas tank is paying a war tax they never voted for with a dollar more per gallon (filling up my tank yesterday cost me $84).
Why Regime Change Rarely Works
Before the war started, thousands of Iranians bravely took to the streets demanding the end of the Islamic regime that has brutalized them for 47 years.
But the goal of U.S.-assisted regime change, without a strategy for succession or any plan to dismantle the IRGC, was never likely to deliver what they were hoping for. Assassinating the Supreme Leader didn't topple the institution or produce regime change. His even more extreme son filled the role within 24 hours (a son whose wife and son were killed in our recent attacks).
We’ve seen this play out before. I know personally how this goes.
Iraq 2003: U.S. removed Sunni Saddam Hussein in three weeks of combat. The following 8 years of instability, sectarian violence, and insurgency cost over 4,400 American lives and over $2 trillion. The country is still not stable. Sunni-led Iraq was the counterbalance of Shia-led Iran, but Iraq is now Shia led.
Libya 2011: NATO helped remove Muammar Gaddafi. Libya has had essentially no functioning government since. Two rival governments, multiple militias, ongoing civil conflict.
The pattern is the same every time: removing a government, even a hostile one, creates a power vacuum. And power vacuums don't fill themselves with democracies. In the case of Iran, it hasn’t even gotten to that point.
The Nuclear Question
Last June, the US and Israel hit Iran's nuclear facilities and declared the program "totally obliterated."
The facilities were damaged and set back, but Iran's enriched uranium stockpile was not destroyed.
So when the February war started, and one of Trump's stated objectives was preventing Iran from getting a nuclear weapon it raised an obvious question. If the summer attack worked, why was it necessary again seven months later?
What exactly was achieved if Iran still has a clear path to nuclear capability and the regime is not weakened in any lasting way other than a change in leadership to a more extreme ayatollah. If anything the IRGC has emerged stronger and Iran's path to nuclear capability remains open.
And we are now absorbing our own economic blows for a war that’s achieved none of the things it set out to accomplish.
When I deployed to Bosnia and Baghdad with the 82nd Airborne, and later when I served in Congress and the Pentagon, the one principle I heard from every serious military and national security professional I ever worked with was this: the quality of a decision is only as good as the quality of the process behind it. We don't run military operations purely on gut instinct. We run them on intelligence assessments, red teams, second and third-order consequence analysis, and a full accounting of every outcome because the costs of getting it wrong don't stay contained to the decision that caused them.
That process didn't happen here. This war was not authorized through Congress as mandated by the Constitution. The War Powers Resolution requires congressional notification within 48 hours of committing forces to hostilities, and Congress has largely looked the other way, bending the knee to a President in their same political party. But the constitutional question is almost secondary to the strategic one. A conflict with direct implications for global energy markets, Indo-Pacific readiness, and munitions stockpiles already strained from years of supporting Ukraine deserved a full congressional debate, not a 90-minute Situation Room meeting where the deadline was self-imposed and the Treasury Secretary wasn't even in the room.
Congress has not been a passive victim here. Too many members on both sides have been content to let the President absorb the political risk without demanding the constitutional accountability that goes with it. That has to change.
I’m hopeful the ceasefire negotiations produce a clean end to this war. But a two-week pause does not undo what the last six weeks produced. We are leaving this conflict with depleted stockpiles, an oil market permanently repriced, and a Strait of Hormuz that was international waters in January but now operating as an Iranian toll booth. The lesson of every military decision made without a clear objective and a defined exit is the same one we keep relearning at enormous cost - including the lives of our sons and daughters in uniform. At some point, Congress has to decide whether it wants to be a co-equal branch of government or a content spectator.
- Patrick

Most importantly, please keep our troops and everyone in the region in your nightly prayers.

Dear Friend, Winning matters. And this year, your State Freedom Caucuses are putting real wins on the board.As legislative sessions wrap up across the country, we’re taking a moment to highlight just a few of the victories our members have secured. There are more victories than we can fit into a single email, so we’ll be sharing additional wins in the weeks ahead.When conservatives keep their promises and lead with principle, results follow.

**RACKING UP THE WINS** The results are coming in from across the country.In **Wyoming** , it was a budget session, which meant non-budget bills required a supermajority just to be considered. The **Wyoming Freedom Caucus** , which controls the House, used that rule to stop bad legislation before it could even move forward.They blocked bills that would have expanded Medicaid (**HB 63** and **HB 64**) and they killed a bill that would create another senseless corporate welfare commission (**SF 126**). They stopped $10 million in subsidies for Big Ag (**SF 109**) and blocked $4.5 billion in spending increases.And they passed a budget that came in 6 percent lower than what the Governor proposed.Your **South Dakota Freedom Caucus** delivered several major victories this year. They sponsored and passed **SB 175** , requiring proof of citizenship to register to vote. While Washington continues to stall on the SAVE Act, South Dakota got it done. The SDFC has also been vocal in calling out Senate Majority Leader John Thune to take action at the federal level. South Dakota has a nasty habit of destroying ballots and other election documents shortly after an election. The SDFC sponsored and passed a bill (**SB 176**) that would preserve those records longer so that citizens can actually audit and review the election results. On spending, they stopped corporate welfare by killing two bills (**SB 239 and SB 234**) that would have subsidized data centers, denying the lieutenant governor the opportunity to cast a tie-breaking vote. And when it came to the state budget, every member voted no and spoke out against it. Last year, they were largely alone in opposing the budget, posting just 13 NO votes. But this year, they brought some of their fellow conservative non-freedom caucus members along, posting 26 NO votes. Recall that the last election cycle, 14 liberal Republicans were voted out of office in the state. Eventually the remaining RINOs in office are going to get the hint that South Dakotans are tired of fake Republicans acting like real conservatives on the campaign trail, but then voting like Democrats once in office. Click on the image below to read about the budget fight. It includes several great quotes from SDFC members.

At issue is the continued use of QR codes to tabulate votes, even though state law prohibits it. The GAFC is demanding a return to hand-marked paper ballots to ensure election integrity.But this is not just about Georgia.It is about the pattern. When legislatures fail to act, your State Freedom Caucuses use every available tool to force the issues that matter.The **Georgia Freedom Caucus** has done this before, calling for a special session to address the actions of Fani Willis after her prosecution of President Trump.Other states have done the same. The **Montana Freedom Caucus** has called for special sessions to ban non-citizens from voting and to cut property taxes.The **Wyoming Freedom Caucus** pushed for a special session to override vetoes on property tax relief, Second Amendment protections, food freedom, and school choice. And the **Missouri Freedom Caucus** called for redistricting, which forced the governor to convene a special session. The legislature then passed a new map that resulted in an additional Republican congressional seat.The message is simple.If "Republican" leaders don't act, State Freedom Caucuses will force action and demand accountability.

And this year, your State Freedom Caucuses are putting real wins on the board.As legislative sessions wrap up across the country, we’re taking a moment to highlight just a few of the victories our members have secured. There are more victories than we can fit into a single email, so we’ll be sharing additional wins in the weeks ahead.When conservatives keep their promises and lead with principle, results follow. | RACKING UP THE WINS The results are coming in from across the country.In Wyoming , it was a budget session, which meant non-budget bills required a supermajority just to be considered. The Wyoming Freedom Caucus , which controls the House, used that rule to stop bad legislation before it could even move forward.They blocked bills that would have expanded Medicaid (HB 63 and HB 64) and they killed a bill that would create another senseless corporate welfare commission (SF 126). They stopped $10 million in subsidies for Big Ag (SF 109) and blocked $4.5 billion in spending increases.And they passed a budget that came in 6 percent lower than what the Governor proposed.Your South Dakota Freedom Caucus delivered several major victories this year. They sponsored and passed SB 175 , requiring proof of citizenship to register to vote. While Washington continues to stall on the SAVE Act, South Dakota got it done. The SDFC has also been vocal in calling out Senate Majority Leader John Thune to take action at the federal level. South Dakota has a nasty habit of destroying ballots and other election documents shortly after an election. The SDFC sponsored and passed a bill (SB 176) that would preserve those records longer so that citizens can actually audit and review the election results. On spending, they stopped corporate welfare by killing two bills (SB 239 and SB 234) that would have subsidized data centers, denying the lieutenant governor the opportunity to cast a tie-breaking vote. And when it came to the state budget, every member voted no and spoke out against it. Last year, they were largely alone in opposing the budget, posting just 13 NO votes. But this year, they brought some of their fellow conservative non-freedom caucus members along, posting 26 NO votes. Recall that the last election cycle, 14 liberal Republicans were voted out of office in the state. Eventually the remaining RINOs in office are going to get the hint that South Dakotans are tired of fake Republicans acting like real conservatives on the campaign trail, but then voting like Democrats once in office. | | Friend, As we close out the first quarter of 2026, I want to take a moment to sincerely **_thank you_** —not just for your support, but for putting your continued trust in me to be your voice in Washington. Out here on the Western Slope, we know what's at stake. Our water. Our lands. Our way of life. These aren't talking points—they're the foundation of our community, and preserving them is the reason I show up to work every single day. Because of you—your conversations, your prayers, your generosity—we are building a movement much bigger than ourselves. A campaign rooted in the values that define rural Colorado: **hard work, stewardship of the land, and an unshakeable commitment to the people who make this region great.** I will never stop fighting to protect Rural Colorado's way of life. Thank you for trusting me to represent you. It’s because of your support that I am confident we will earn another term and keep fighting for the Western Slope for years to come.
---
| | God bless,

clean_body: A progress report| | | | | Friend, As we close out the first quarter of 2026, I want to take a moment to sincerely thank you —not just for your support, but for putting your continued trust in me to be your voice in Washington. Out here on the Western Slope, we know what's at stake. Our water. Our lands. Our way of life. These aren't talking points—they're the foundation of our community, and preserving them is the reason I show up to work every single day. Because of you—your conversations, your prayers, your generosity—we are building a movement much bigger than ourselves. A campaign rooted in the values that define rural Colorado: hard work, stewardship of the land, and an unshakeable commitment to the people who make this region great. I will never stop fighting to protect Rural Colorado's way of life. Thank you for trusting me to represent you. A recent _Michigan Advance_ investigation revealed just _how easily Mike Rogers is bought and sold by banking and financial industries_ — to the tune of _millions of dollars_ for his Senate campaign.
Rogers said that he wants to sit on the Senate Banking Committee — the very committee that is supposed to oversee financial institutions. That would give him direct influence over legislation that his big donors care about most. And direct power to screw over regular people to favor those donors.
This is a pattern for Rogers — he’s had Big Banks propping him up for a long time. When he was in Congress, he was in the top 11% of lawmakers receiving contributions from bankers and investors.
His voting record, from the state legislature to Congress, consistently shows him putting the interests of big banks and corporations ahead of his constituents.
**It’s pretty simple: Mike Rogers only cares about Wall Street and special interests.**

| **OFFICIAL JANEPAC SURVEY** **We’re surveying JanePAC supporters all across the country for their input on how to hold Big Oil and Big Gas accountable.** **[Lawsuits are one of the main tools we have to ensure fossil fuel companies pay their fair share for the harm they’ve caused. Can you take this two-minute survey to share your opinions with us?](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/129197676/613578516/899194069?refcode=ea.ab7937b9-f734-f111-8ef2-000d3a14b640&ms=ea.ab7937b9-f734-f111-8ef2-000d3a14b640&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9FQS9FQTAxNi8xLzk2NzgyIiwNCiAgIkRpc3RyaWJ1dGlvblVuaXF1ZUlkIjogImFiNzkzN2I5LWY3MzQtZjExMS04ZWYyLTAwMGQzYTE0YjY0MCIsDQogICJFbWFpbEFkZHJlc3MiOiAiZHB3aWxsaXM2N0BnbWFpbC5jb20iDQp9&hmac=SueZYKIQNxUoQ77VrkBgrRmjhgoK7Wv5tmmPpY9ib7o=&emci=d3c9b9ca-3234-f111-8ef2-000d3a14b640&emdi=ab7937b9-f734-f111-8ef2-000d3a14b640&ceid=4823105)** | [TAKE THE SURVEY](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/129197680/613578518/899194069?refcode=ea.ab7937b9-f734-f111-8ef2-000d3a14b640&ms=ea.ab7937b9-f734-f111-8ef2-000d3a14b640&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9FQS9FQTAxNi8xLzk2NzgyIiwNCiAgIkRpc3RyaWJ1dGlvblVuaXF1ZUlkIjogImFiNzkzN2I5LWY3MzQtZjExMS04ZWYyLTAwMGQzYTE0YjY0MCIsDQogICJFbWFpbEFkZHJlc3MiOiAiZHB3aWxsaXM2N0BnbWFpbC5jb20iDQp9&hmac=SueZYKIQNxUoQ77VrkBgrRmjhgoK7Wv5tmmPpY9ib7o=&emci=d3c9b9ca-3234-f111-8ef2-000d3a14b640&emdi=ab7937b9-f734-f111-8ef2-000d3a14b640&ceid=4823105)
---
Republicans are working overtime to help the fossil fuel industry dodge accountability, and we can’t afford to ignore it.
**Utah just became the first state in the country to pass a law shielding fossil fuel companies from facing the consequences of their pollution through climate lawsuits.** And now, Republicans in Oklahoma, Louisiana, Tennessee, and Iowa are racing to do the same.
Communities across the country are paying the price for deadly floods, fires, storms, and extreme heat. The fossil fuel industry knew its products, like plastic and toxic forever chemicals, were fueling the climate crisis and endangering public health, lied about it for decades, and kept cashing in.
Instead of demanding accountability, Republicans are rushing to protect the companies responsible.
**That is outrageous. And it’s exactly why electing climate fighters — _especially strong Democratic attorneys general_ — is a matter of urgency.**
When Washington is paralyzed by gridlock, attorneys general are often our last line of defense. They are the ones who can take polluters to court and fight back when Big Oil and its allies try to put themselves above the law.
**That is exactly the kind of fearless work our JanePAC climate champ, California AG Rob Bonta, is doing right now.** Rob is leading a coalition of blue states in suing Trump’s EPA after it repealed the endangerment finding — one of the most important legal tools for regulating greenhouse gas pollution.
**But the only way we beat back this kind of corporate power is by building people-power _now._ And that means hearing directly from the grassroots supporters like you who make this movement possible:** **[Do you support lawsuits as a way to hold fossil fuel companies accountable for the harm they’ve caused?](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/129197684/613578521/899194069?refcode=ea.ab7937b9-f734-f111-8ef2-000d3a14b640&ms=ea.ab7937b9-f734-f111-8ef2-000d3a14b640&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9FQS9FQTAxNi8xLzk2NzgyIiwNCiAgIkRpc3RyaWJ1dGlvblVuaXF1ZUlkIjogImFiNzkzN2I5LWY3MzQtZjExMS04ZWYyLTAwMGQzYTE0YjY0MCIsDQogICJFbWFpbEFkZHJlc3MiOiAiZHB3aWxsaXM2N0BnbWFpbC5jb20iDQp9&hmac=SueZYKIQNxUoQ77VrkBgrRmjhgoK7Wv5tmmPpY9ib7o=&emci=d3c9b9ca-3234-f111-8ef2-000d3a14b640&emdi=ab7937b9-f734-f111-8ef2-000d3a14b640&ceid=4823105)** | [**YES**](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/129197689/613578524/899194069?refcode=ea.ab7937b9-f734-f111-8ef2-000d3a14b640&ms=ea.ab7937b9-f734-f111-8ef2-000d3a14b640&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9FQS9FQTAxNi8xLzk2NzgyIiwNCiAgIkRpc3RyaWJ1dGlvblVuaXF1ZUlkIjogImFiNzkzN2I5LWY3MzQtZjExMS04ZWYyLTAwMGQzYTE0YjY0MCIsDQogICJFbWFpbEFkZHJlc3MiOiAiZHB3aWxsaXM2N0BnbWFpbC5jb20iDQp9&hmac=SueZYKIQNxUoQ77VrkBgrRmjhgoK7Wv5tmmPpY9ib7o=&emci=d3c9b9ca-3234-f111-8ef2-000d3a14b640&emdi=ab7937b9-f734-f111-8ef2-000d3a14b640&ceid=4823105) | [**NO**](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/129197692/613578528/899194069?refcode=ea.ab7937b9-f734-f111-8ef2-000d3a14b640&ms=ea.ab7937b9-f734-f111-8ef2-000d3a14b640&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9FQS9FQTAxNi8xLzk2NzgyIiwNCiAgIkRpc3RyaWJ1dGlvblVuaXF1ZUlkIjogImFiNzkzN2I5LWY3MzQtZjExMS04ZWYyLTAwMGQzYTE0YjY0MCIsDQogICJFbWFpbEFkZHJlc3MiOiAiZHB3aWxsaXM2N0BnbWFpbC5jb20iDQp9&hmac=SueZYKIQNxUoQ77VrkBgrRmjhgoK7Wv5tmmPpY9ib7o=&emci=d3c9b9ca-3234-f111-8ef2-000d3a14b640&emdi=ab7937b9-f734-f111-8ef2-000d3a14b640&ceid=4823105)

clean_body: Tell us where you stand on holding fossil fuel companies accountable. | | OFFICIAL JANEPAC SURVEY We’re surveying JanePAC supporters all across the country for their input on how to hold Big Oil and Big Gas accountable. | Republicans are working overtime to help the fossil fuel industry dodge accountability, and we can’t afford to ignore it. Utah just became the first state in the country to pass a law shielding fossil fuel companies from facing the consequences of their pollution through climate lawsuits. And now, Republicans in Oklahoma, Louisiana, Tennessee, and Iowa are racing to do the same. Communities across the country are paying the price for deadly floods, fires, storms, and extreme heat. The fossil fuel industry knew its products, like plastic and toxic forever chemicals, were fueling the climate crisis and endangering public health, lied about it for decades, and kept cashing in. Instead of demanding accountability, Republicans are rushing to protect the companies responsible. That is outrageous. And it’s exactly why electing climate fighters — especially strong Democratic attorneys general — is a matter of urgency. When Washington is paralyzed by gridlock, attorneys general are often our last line of defense. They are the ones who can take polluters to court and fight back when Big Oil and its allies try to put themselves above the law. That is exactly the kind of fearless work our JanePAC climate champ, California AG Rob Bonta, is doing right now. Rob is leading a coalition of blue states in suing Trump’s EPA after it repealed the endangerment finding — one of the most important legal tools for regulating greenhouse gas pollution. But the only way we beat back this kind of corporate power is by building people-power now. And that means hearing directly from the grassroots supporters like you who make this movement possible: | | ---|--- Thanks for making your voice heard. — Team JanePAC | = | = = Follow along: | | | | | ---|---|---|---|---|--- Paid for by Jane Fonda Climate PAC, not authorized by any candidate or candidate’s committee. body:
Join us for Immigrant Day of Resilience | | | Peter, Every moment is an organizing opportunity, every person a potential activist, and every minute a chance to change the world. **This includes YOU, too.** Today, Dolores Huerta is a renowned labor leader and civil rights activist. She led negotiations in the historical Delano Grape Strike and organized her community to major victories, including higher wages and protections against pesticides for farm workers. But, before all this, Dolores Huerta was eleven years old, watching her Japanese American classmates disappear from their classrooms and sent to internment camps. She was a 24-year-old teacher in a classroom filled with the children of farmworkers, realizing that educators alone don’t have the resources to support their students when they show up to school in need of food or better clothes. And, she was only 25 when she began organizing in her community in Stockton, California. Family by family, house by house, she made it her mission to make her neighbors aware of their power to create change. **Every year, on April 10, we honor Dolores Huerta Day as a reminder that power exists within each one of us to build the future we need.** Like Dolores, you may have encountered situations that made you aware of the challenges your community faces. In the last year alone, we’ve witnessed immigration agents unleashing violence and harm in our communities. **Just like Dolores, you have the power to turn these painful moments into an opportunity to organize your friends and neighbors, and together, build the future we need. ✊🧡** Ready to tap into that power?**[Join us on Wednesday, April 15, at 6:30 pm ET/ 5:30 pm CT at our “Live, Laugh, This includes YOU, too. Today, Dolores Huerta is a renowned labor leader and civil rights activist. She led negotiations in the historical Delano Grape Strike and organized her community to major victories, including higher wages and protections against pesticides for farm workers. But, before all this, Dolores Huerta was eleven years old, watching her Japanese American classmates disappear from their classrooms and sent to internment camps. She was a 24-year-old teacher in a classroom filled with the children of farmworkers, realizing that educators alone don’t have the resources to support their students when they show up to school in need of food or better clothes. And, she was only 25 when she began organizing in her community in Stockton, California. Family by family, house by house, she made it her mission to make her neighbors aware of their power to create change. Every year, on April 10, we honor Dolores Huerta Day as a reminder that power exists within each one of us to build the future we need. Like Dolores, you may have encountered situations that made you aware of the challenges your community faces. In the last year alone, we’ve witnessed immigration agents unleashing violence and harm in our communities. Just like Dolores, you have the power to turn these painful moments into an opportunity to organize your friends and neighbors, and together, build the future we need. ✊🧡 Ready to tap into that power? ** **Together, we are power. Generation after generation, from farmworkers who led mass boycotts to our neighbors now standing up for immigrants in the face of violent ICE raids, our communities have stood united to protect one another. The Iran war has been in a ceasefire since Wednesday, with negotiations in Islamabad set for this weekend. Iran conducted missile and drone strikes against Kuwait, Bahrain, and the UAE within hours of the ceasefire announcement. I hope and pray it holds. But before we call this over, it's worth being honest about where things actually stand.
The global energy market has been disrupted in unprecedented ways by this war.
Before this war started, ships passed through the Strait of Hormuz freely -- a waterway carrying roughly 20 percent of the world's oil supply. Over 100 vessels a day passed with no coordination required, no fees, and no permission needed from anyone.
That's gone now.
Iran's foreign minister announced that passage through the Strait would now require "coordination with Iran's Armed Forces," with fees of up to $2 million per vessel -- a structure Iran's parliament has already moved to codify into law. A waterway that Iran had no formal control over six weeks ago is now, functionally, a tollbooth the Islamic Republic operates. Iran is capping transit at 15 vessels a day and has published routes that funnel traffic into Revolutionary Guard-controlled water. Beyond those designated routes, at least a dozen underwater mines have been reported.
Iran entered this war under maximum sanctions with its supreme leader dead. Now, they're demanding that the United States withdraw all military forces from the region, accept continued uranium enrichment, and pay reparations through ship transit fees. Those demands will almost certainly soften in negotiations, but the fact that they're the opening position of a country whose military was largely destroyed tells you everything about how the leverage actually played out.
This outcome was foreseeable.
Earlier this week, the _[New York Times](https://substack.com/redirect/7fba79a1-143c-419f-8263-ade21a872816?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)_ published what may be the most consequential piece of national security journalism since the Iraq War intelligence failures were laid bare. Jonathan Swan and Maggie Haberman, drawing on roughly 1,000 interviews for their forthcoming book on Trump's second term, reconstructed the Situation Room meetings that took the United States into war with Iran. The details of how this war started are jarring and should concern every American, regardless of where they stand politically.
What the Times reporting makes impossible to ignore is the process by which this specific decision was made.
On February 11, Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu came to the White House and delivered a four-part pitch: kill the Supreme Leader, destroy Iran's missile program, spark a popular uprising, and install a secular government. The CIA director reviewed the pitch overnight, and the next morning, he used one word to describe the regime-change scenario: "farcical." Secretary Rubio agreed, though he supported the narrower goal of degrading Iran's military capability rather than regime change.
Despite pushback, President Trump decided to go through with it, partly convinced he could repeat the swift Venezuela operation. That overconfidence has cost 13 American servicemembers their lives and left 380 more wounded, along with thousands of casualties across the region, including civilians.

# **The War Tax**
This war has been an expensive campaign, and the math tells the story plainly.
Iran builds a drone for roughly $20,000. The United States fires a $2 million interceptor missile to knock it down, then does it again, and again, for weeks, against an adversary that sources components through Russia and China and rebuilds faster than we can replenish.
That's a 100-to-1 cost exchange sustained at scale against a country with an essentially unlimited supply of cheap materials and outside help filling the gaps.
The war has cost at least $12 billion so far and counting. Oil, which was around $70 a barrel before the war, shot past $100. Every American filling up their gas tank is paying a war tax they never voted for, with a dollar more per gallon (filling up my tank yesterday cost me $84).
# **Why Regime Change Rarely Works**
Before the war started, thousands of Iranians bravely took to the streets demanding the end of the Islamic regime that has brutalized them for 47 years.
But the goal of U.S.-assisted regime change, without a strategy for succession or any plan to dismantle the IRGC, was never likely to deliver what they were hoping for. Assassinating the Supreme Leader didn't topple the institution or produce regime change. His son Mojtaba, considered more hardline than his father and more deeply tied to the IRGC, filled the role within days.
We've seen this play out before. I know personally how this goes.
**Iraq 2003** : The U.S. removed Saddam Hussein in three weeks of combat. The following eight years of instability, sectarian violence, and insurgency cost over 4,400 American lives and over $2 trillion, and the country is still not stable. Saddam's Sunni-led government had served as a regional counterbalance to Shia-led Iran for decades -- that counterbalance is now gone, and Iraq has moved firmly into Iran's orbit.
**Libya 2011** : NATO helped remove Muammar Gaddafi. Libya has had essentially no functioning government since -- two rival administrations, multiple militias, and ongoing civil conflict.
The pattern is the same every time: removing a government, even a hostile one, creates a power vacuum. And power vacuums don't fill themselves with democracies. In the case of Iran, it hasn't even gotten to that point.
# **The Nuclear Question**
Last June, the U.S. and Israel hit Iran's nuclear facilities and declared the program "totally obliterated."
The facilities were damaged and set back, but Iran's enriched uranium stockpile was not destroyed.
So when the February war started, and one of Trump's stated objectives was preventing Iran from getting a nuclear weapon, it raised an obvious question. If the summer attack worked, why was it necessary again seven months later?
What exactly was achieved if Iran still has a clear path to nuclear capability and the regime is not weakened in any lasting way other than a change in leadership to a more extreme ayatollah? If anything, the IRGC has emerged stronger, and Iran's path to nuclear capability remains open.
And we are now absorbing our own economic blows for a war that's achieved none of the things it set out to accomplish.
When I deployed to Bosnia and Baghdad with the 82nd Airborne, and later when I served in Congress and the Pentagon, the one principle I heard from every serious military and national security professional I ever worked with was this: the quality of a decision is only as good as the quality of the process behind it. We don't run military operations purely on gut instinct. We run them on intelligence assessments, red teams, second and third-order consequence analysis, and a full accounting of every outcome because the costs of getting it wrong don't stay contained to the decision that caused them.
That process didn't happen here. This war was not authorized through Congress as mandated by the Constitution. The War Powers Resolution requires congressional notification within 48 hours of committing forces to hostilities, and Congress has largely looked the other way, bending the knee to a President in their same political party. But the constitutional question is almost secondary to the strategic one. A conflict with direct implications for global energy markets, Indo-Pacific readiness, and munitions stockpiles already strained from years of supporting Ukraine deserved a full congressional debate, not a 90-minute Situation Room meeting where the deadline was self-imposed and the Treasury Secretary wasn't even in the room.
Congress has not been a passive victim here. Too many members on both sides have been content to let the President absorb the political risk without demanding the constitutional accountability that goes with it. That has to change.
I'm hopeful the ceasefire negotiations produce a clean end to this war. But a two-week pause does not undo what the last six weeks produced. We are leaving this conflict with depleted stockpiles, an oil market permanently repriced, and a Strait of Hormuz that was international waters in January and is now operating as an Iranian toll booth. The lesson of every military decision made without a clear objective and a defined exit is the same one we keep relearning at enormous cost, including the lives of our sons and daughters in uniform. At some point, Congress has to decide whether it wants to be a coequal branch of government or a spectator.

The war has cost at least $12 billion so far and counting. Oil, which was around $70 a barrel before the war, shot past $100. Every American filling up their gas tank is paying a war tax they never voted for, with a dollar more per gallon (filling up my tank yesterday cost me $84). Why Regime Change Rarely Works Before the war started, thousands of Iranians bravely took to the streets demanding the end of the Islamic regime that has brutalized them for 47 years. But the goal of U.S.-assisted regime change, without a strategy for succession or any plan to dismantle the IRGC, was never likely to deliver what they were hoping for. Assassinating the Supreme Leader didn't topple the institution or produce regime change. His son Mojtaba, considered more hardline than his father and more deeply tied to the IRGC, filled the role within days. We've seen this play out before. I know personally how this goes. Iraq 2003 : The U.S. removed Saddam Hussein in three weeks of combat. The following eight years of instability, sectarian violence, and insurgency cost over 4,400 American lives and over $2 trillion, and the country is still not stable. Saddam's Sunni-led government had served as a regional counterbalance to Shia-led Iran for decades -- that counterbalance is now gone, and Iraq has moved firmly into Iran's orbit. Libya 2011 : NATO helped remove Muammar Gaddafi. Libya has had essentially no functioning government since -- two rival administrations, multiple militias, and ongoing civil conflict. The pattern is the same every time: removing a government, even a hostile one, creates a power vacuum. And power vacuums don't fill themselves with democracies. In the case of Iran, it hasn't even gotten to that point. The Nuclear Question** Last June, the U.S. and Israel hit Iran's nuclear facilities and declared the program "totally obliterated." The facilities were damaged and set back, but Iran's enriched uranium stockpile was not destroyed. So when the February war started, and one of Trump's stated objectives was preventing Iran from getting a nuclear weapon, it raised an obvious question. If the summer attack worked, why was it necessary again seven months later? What exactly was achieved if Iran still has a clear path to nuclear capability and the regime is not weakened in any lasting way other than a change in leadership to a more extreme ayatollah? If anything, the IRGC has emerged stronger, and Iran's path to nuclear capability remains open. And we are now absorbing our own economic blows for a war that's achieved none of the things it set out to accomplish. When I deployed to Bosnia and Baghdad with the 82nd Airborne, and later when I served in Congress and the Pentagon, the one principle I heard from every serious military and national security professional I ever worked with was this: the quality of a decision is only as good as the quality of the process behind it. We don't run military operations purely on gut instinct. We run them on intelligence assessments, red teams, second and third-order consequence analysis, and a full accounting of every outcome because the costs of getting it wrong don't stay contained to the decision that caused them. That process didn't happen here. This war was not authorized through Congress as mandated by the Constitution. The War Powers Resolution requires congressional notification within 48 hours of committing forces to hostilities, and Congress has largely looked the other way, bending the knee to a President in their same political party. But the constitutional question is almost secondary to the strategic one. A conflict with direct implications for global energy markets, Indo-Pacific readiness, and munitions stockpiles already strained from years of supporting Ukraine deserved a full congressional debate, not a 90-minute Situation Room meeting where the deadline was self-imposed and the Treasury Secretary wasn't even in the room. Congress has not been a passive victim here. Too many members on both sides have been content to let the President absorb the political risk without demanding the constitutional accountability that goes with it. That has to change. I'm hopeful the ceasefire negotiations produce a clean end to this war. But a two-week pause does not undo what the last six weeks produced. We are leaving this conflict with depleted stockpiles, an oil market permanently repriced, and a Strait of Hormuz that was international waters in January and is now operating as an Iranian toll booth. The lesson of every military decision made without a clear objective and a defined exit is the same one we keep relearning at enormous cost, including the lives of our sons and daughters in uniform. At some point, Congress has to decide whether it wants to be a coequal branch of government or a spectator. Donald Trump is desperate to avoid historic losses for Republicans this November. But instead of working to earn votes by doing things the American people support, he’s racing to rig the rules. That’s why — just last week — he signed a blatantly unconstitutional executive order trying to restrict mail voting. And that’s why we have to keep fighting back for equal access to the ballot box. **[If you’re outraged and able to push back with a donation right now, please chip in to help prevent voter suppression, electing voting rights champions, and fight for free and fair elections. Your support helps make sure we’re able to respond to new threats like this executive order at a moment’s notice.](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/129200206/613581314/-1370916003?refcode=emm_ff_20260410_T1_TrumpEONOR_v1s1&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQNDMvMS84ODQ1MCIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICIxMTE5YzBkMy1mOTM0LWYxMTEtOGVmMi0wMDBkM2ExNGI2NDAiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=MfYionSDS2Q3kNXH2E4SMw2GCKnVZpj3yU9g94I0SI4=)** Trump’s order sets out to create lists of citizens eligible to vote in each state, mandate that mail ballots only be sent to voters on approved lists, prioritize investigations into ballots sent to ineligible voters, and threaten to cut off federal funding for states that don’t comply with the new requirements. **Here are a few key points you can bring up to highlight the absurdity — and the autocratic origins — of this order:**
* **Just weeks ago, Trump himself voted by mail** in Florida. Now he wants to restrict that same right for millions of Americans.
* Three federal judges already blocked provisions of a similar Trump order trying to change how elections are run — because **presidents don’t have the power to do this.**
* Naturally,**this tracks back to Putin.** Last summer, Trump declared that he’d try to ban mail voting after hearing from Putin that supposedly “it’s impossible to have mail-in voting and have an honest election.”
* But **mail voting fraud is virtually nonexistent** — only 0.000043% of all mail ballots cast according to a Brookings Institution Report. And when Georgia’s Republican Secretary of State audited 8.2 million voters in 2024, he only found a 0.002% rate of possible irregularities.

Trump’s in for a tough court fight. clean_body: Here’s what you need to know: | | | BREAKING: “Trump signs sweeping order attacking mail-in voting” —Democracy Docket We knew this was on the horizon. Donald Trump is desperate to avoid historic losses for Republicans this November. But instead of working to earn votes by doing things the American people support, he’s racing to rig the rules. That’s why — just last week — he signed a blatantly unconstitutional executive order trying to restrict mail voting. And that’s why we have to keep fighting back for equal access to the ballot box. = Trump’s order sets out to create lists of citizens eligible to vote in each state, mandate that mail ballots only be sent to voters on approved lists, prioritize investigations into ballots sent to ineligible voters, and threaten to cut off federal funding for states that don’t comply with the new requirements. Here are a few key points you can bring up to highlight the absurdity — and the autocratic origins — of this order: Just weeks ago, Trump himself voted by mail in Florida. Now he wants to restrict that same right for millions of Americans. Three federal judges already blocked provisions of a similar Trump order trying to change how elections are run — because presidents don’t have the power to do this. Naturally,this tracks back to Putin. Last summer, Trump declared that he’d try to ban mail voting after hearing from Putin that supposedly “it’s impossible to have mail-in voting and have an honest election.” But mail voting fraud is virtually nonexistent — only 0.000043% of all mail ballots cast according to a Brookings Institution Report. And when Georgia’s Republican Secretary of State audited 8.2 million voters in 2024, he only found a 0.002% rate of possible irregularities. Trump’s in for a tough court fight. And we know what we need to do: stay laser-focused on our mission to make sure the American people are free to make their voices heard this November. = Thank you for everything you do to power this work. Socialist Mayor Zohran Mamdani Locks New Yorkers Out of America's 250th Birthday Celebration in Times Square

New York City's socialist Mayor Zohran Mamdani is facing massive backlash after blocking ordinary Americans from celebrating the nation's 250th birthday in Times Square. The mayor has denied nine permits for public access to a planned ball drop event commemorating America's semiquincentennial, transforming what should be a free patriotic celebration into an exclusive ticketed affair.

A viral video from Times Square captures the raw frustration of New Yorkers who discovered they've been locked out of their own nation's birthday party. The footage shows residents and tourists expressing disbelief that their tax-funded public space has been cordoned off for the wealthy while working Americans are told to buy tickets or stay home.

Mamdani issued an emergency order citing security concerns for the 2026 FIFA World Cup, but critics see this as prioritizing international soccer over American patriotism. The decision effectively hands Times Square—the heart of New York and symbol of American celebration—over to foreign interests while shutting out the very Americans whose ancestors built this republic.

Interviews from the scene reveal the depth of public anger. One New Yorker called Mamdani a "famous communist" who "won't allow people to come up and see and celebrate 250th years for the U.S." He added bluntly that the mayor "needs to go" because "he's anti-America."

Another resident questioned whether this was still America, asking "Is this really New York? Where we at?" A woman described the exclusion as "really sad" and "very silly," arguing the celebration "should be allowed to be something with celebrating."

Even a Canadian visitor was shocked by the anti-American hostility, noting "it never happened in Canada" and insisting "the public should be allowed to go." An excited American who planned to attend expressed frustration: "I was kind of excited to come down here for that. But, you know, I'm not buying a ticket. It's ridiculous."

The controversy highlights a deeper problem with progressive governance in America's major cities. While Mamdani caters to international events and wealthy elites, he treats American patriots as second-class citizens in their own country. This is the same mayor who has pushed socialist policies that have driven businesses out of New York while making the city increasingly unaffordable for working families.

America's 250th birthday on July 4, 2026, represents a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity for Americans to gather and celebrate the founding principles that created the greatest republic in human history. Times Square has hosted countless celebrations of American achievement, from victory parades to New Year's Eve gatherings where millions have celebrated together as one people.

But under Mamdani's socialist leadership, even this sacred tradition gets sacrificed on the altar of globalism. The mayor's decision to prioritize World Cup security over American celebration reveals his true priorities—and they aren't with the American people who elected him.

The backlash on social media continues to grow as Americans across the country learn about Mamdani's anti-patriotic power grab. Conservative voices are calling this exactly what it is: a deliberate attack on American tradition by a mayor who seems more comfortable serving foreign interests than his own constituents.

This isn't just about one celebration. It's about whether Americans still have the right to gather freely in their own public spaces to honor the republic that guarantees those very freedoms. When socialist politicians can unilaterally decide that working Americans don't deserve access to their own nation's birthday party, we've lost something fundamental about what makes America great.

Mamdani's decision stands as a perfect symbol of progressive contempt for ordinary Americans and their patriotic values. While the mayor rolls out red carpets for international soccer fans, he tells American families they need to pay up or stay home from their own country's most important milestone celebration.

https://www.everyaction.com/ [https://www.everyaction.com/]
Weekly Montgomery
Volunteer Round-Up
72 Days Until the Primary Election
This weekly email goes out to all of our hard-working volunteers and covers local events, canvassing, phone banks, text banks, and postcard writing!
Thank you for being what makes this campaign special. We hope to see you at all of the events below!
image of ... [https://prod.cdn.everyaction.com/images/van/NGP/NGP59/1/109172/images/fired%20up%20email.png]
Office Opening and Canvass
Saturday, April 18th, 11 AM - 2 PM
We've opened our new Gaithersburg headquarters, and we're celebrating by doing what this campaign does best: getting out into the community and talking to voters.
Join us Saturday for an office opening rally (11–12), where you'll hear directly from Congresswoman Delaney and community leaders about why MD-6 is worth fighting for and why this moment matters. Then we're hitting the doors together for a canvass launch (12–2) to build the grassroots energy that will power us to the polls!
MD-6 voters are energized. Our volunteer base is growing. And the momentum is real. Every door knocked, every conversation had, moves us closer to June.
Come be part of it!
Sign Up Here [https://www.mobilize.us/aprilmcclaindelaneyforcongress/event/933949/]
(Virtual) Phone Banks
Montgomery County Phone Banks Sign Up [https://www.mobilize.us/aprilmcclaindelaneyforcongress/event/934939/]
Every Thursday night, 6-8 , until Election Night, we will have a virtual and in-person phone bank to turn out supporters and recruit more volunteers!
Either come on into the office or join from the comfort of your own home .
All you need is a phone and the willingness to make some calls. Hope to see you there!

My race has become the _**[MOST TARGETED](https://email.updates.conservativeinnovation.com/c/eJyUkM1uhCAURp8Gdxj-RF2waDox6WK6bJcG4eqQIBBAJ_P2jU36AN3dxcm5J9_3fb5r513YPvUOypxuzmV2NoZ6lEN7_yoQ7A6l6A2KnxlhEhOBKbk42lhlrOSsAUX7vhsEpYQ2D7WaZbHLyq1cAcQoRis7M7CuG8ZFLgNrnLpMRFBCe0K5aJeOSM4NNSOIQYgRCXIkqyuU1sRQIJ-6uhNcCPG6YmhN3BuvHrWmgvgbYhNiUwFzZGifLmSwF4HYtLxyDNjGoL0teI0Zb_GEHGJGbLIx4JRLwrBr57HJrjqjPT4pLhSnmBCfjrrP1SB-e__6YPivGzGZr2_ZhQ3xW80HNFnZ9HTeuyJ7JMh2OX876_-XPRX7CQAA__9T-IkB "MOST TARGETED")**_ race in the nation, because Democrats know if they take Florida from us, there's nothing they can't take.

But Democrats aren't slowing down--**they 're escalating.**

That's why I'm reaching out to you right now with urgency.

I know how much you've done, and I hate asking again, but if I'm being honest:

So I'm asking: Can I ask you to chip in ANY AMOUNT to support my race?

### Accountability, strength, and what the post-Trump era actually requires
| | [Mike Nellis](https://substack.com/@mikenellis)

So I was asked on a podcast the other day if we're going to see a return to civility, empathy, and kindness whenever we reach the inevitable post-Trump America--when he's finally gone or at least becomes so irrelevant that we can, God, maybe ignore him. And I think that's a fascinating question. It's been sitting in my mind for the last couple of days.
In the moment, I said yes, because I believe the vast majority of Americans--including a lot of people who voted for Donald Trump, many of whom are now regretting that decision--are sick of this moment, where some of the worst voices in our society are dominating the discourse and dragging the country down.
* * *
**Today 's rant is sponsored by Ground News.**
I've been paying more attention to how differently the same story gets covered depending on where you read it--especially lately, when everything feels optimized for speed and outrage instead of context.
Take this one--over 200 outlets covered Trump criticizing NATO's response around Iran.
**CNN** frames it as _" Trump_ is _not listening to experts " as tensions escalate._
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/8a8cc399-ee92-46ad-be53-263e71da9af2?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
**New York Post** states he's _" calling NATO members 'cowards' for not stepping up."_
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/8a8cc399-ee92-46ad-be53-263e71da9af2?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Same story--completely different narratives.

That's why I use Ground News. It pulls together 50,000+ sources so you can compare coverage side by side, see political bias, who owns the sources you're reading, how reliable they are and understand how framing changes the story.

You can literally watch how the left vs right headline the same event--and what each side emphasizes (or leaves out).

They also highlight stories you might be missing entirely in their Blindspot Feed which shows you stories that are disproportionately reported by either side of the political spectrum.

I've been a paying user since before they ever sponsored Endless Urgency. I use it because it makes it a lot harder to be misled. They're completely subscriber funded so there are no corporate interests pushing a narrative on what you see.

See the full picture, instead of just one angle with Ground News. [Subscribe](https://substack.com/redirect/a9cfb3ac-a39a-45b7-8c2d-d98e8420a14b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
* * *
People are exhausted. What looks like apathy isn't apathy--it's overload. There's so much chaos and noise that people have gone numb just to keep up. But that numbness isn't permanent. When the pressure lifts, people are going to feel all of this more clearly. And that's when empathy and kindness are going to matter most--when people are trying to process what happened and start putting things back together. We're going to need people to step up and be part of the solution.
And I look forward to that moment because, as I've said before when I've debated conservatives on their shows, I don't hate them. I don't hate people who voted for Donald Trump. I'm mad at them. I don't understand them. But I don't like the coarseness of our politics. I don't like waking up every morning and writing a "good fucking morning" tweet. It doesn't feel good. As much as the engagement is great, it feels cheap for the discourse to operate that way.
I want us to get back to a politics that's about improving people's lives--having real debates, but actually solving problems. And I think we can get there. But there's an important caveat.
A return to empathy or kindness should not be used to force some kind of bland D.C. moderation. It should not become an excuse to forgive and forget the corruption, the chaos, and the damage that's been done.
The clearest example is Gerald Ford pardoning Richard Nixon in the name of national unity. I don't think that made the country stronger. I think we'd be in a different place today if a president had actually been held accountable.
We've seen this pattern before. We didn't prosecute the people who devastated millions of lives during the Wall Street financial crisis. We're still not prosecuting people tied to the Epstein files.
We can be kind. We can be empathetic. We can love our neighbors--people who are just trying to survive, people who've made decisions we don't understand. But that empathy cannot come at the expense of accountability.
I worry about two paths from here.
The first is that Democrats try so hard to win that they become a mirror image of Republicans--driven by grievance, focused on anger, more interested in pissing people off than actually helping anyone. The moment the party stops trying to improve people's lives--even imperfectly--I'm registering as an independent.
The second is more subtle, and maybe more dangerous. We elect a Democrat in '28, everyone exhales, and people tune out again. Civility returns--but so does a lack of accountability.
We've heard this before: time to move on, don't look backward, focus on healing. No. We can't do that again. What's actually good for the country is accountability.
Right now, the country feels adrift. Part of that is because we're not holding the right people accountable. We over-penalize low-level offenses, but we don't go after white-collar crime. There's an entire class of people who can abuse kids and get away with it. We haven't even prosecuted the people who helped traffic them--and the DOJ has the information to act.
* * *
_**Mid-rant note:**_**this section is sponsored by Ground News.**
I've started paying more attention to how the same story can feel completely different depending on who's reporting it. Ground News makes that easy to see by showing coverage from across the political spectrum and pointing out what certain outlets leave out.
My team and I use it because it helps cut through the noise.
**[If you want a clearer view of what's actually going on, check out Ground News ->](https://substack.com/redirect/8a8cc399-ee92-46ad-be53-263e71da9af2?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**
_Give it a try!_
[ Subscribe](https://substack.com/redirect/a9cfb3ac-a39a-45b7-8c2d-d98e8420a14b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
* * *
We can't turn away again. Civility cannot become a way to avoid hard decisions instead of a foundation for making them. That kind of D.C. thinking is more about protecting the cocktail party circuit than delivering for the public.
We should show empathy and kindness to our fellow Americans--including people who were misled or taken advantage of, yes, even people who voted for Donald Trump. That doesn't mean you don't get to be mad. I'm mad. I'm still mad at MAGA influencers who flipped overnight but won't admit the role they played.
But empathy is not a pass.
There are people in this administration, in Trump's orbit, who have stolen from the American people, gotten people killed, and covered up serious crimes. They must be held accountable--period. Not just for justice, but because failing to act tells the next group in power they can get away with the same thing.
And even if some of them are pardoned on the way out, that doesn't change the obligation to pursue the truth.
So whoever earns my vote in the 2028 primary has to do two things.
First, lay out a real vision for the future. How do we rebuild this economy so it actually works for average Americans--not corporations or the untouchable elite, but working people? What does the American dream look like in a world shaped by AI, robotics, and constant technological change?
Second, show me what accountability actually looks like--and make me believe it. Investigations? Hearings? DOJ action? I want specifics. Real oversight, subpoenas, independent investigations, and stronger guardrails that can't be ignored.
How do we rein in executive power so we never end up here again? How do we confront corruption and abuses of power instead of brushing them aside?
That means strengthening the law. It's been too weak. We have to reassert Congress as a co-equal branch of government.
I'm not going to support a technocrat who says the right things and does nothing with teeth. On some level, that's how I feel about the Biden administration. I love Joe Biden, but I don't think they did enough--and that's part of how we ended up back here, in a situation worse than Trump's first term.
We've tried that version of "normal." It doesn't hold.
There has to be strength behind the empathy. Consequences behind the rhetoric. Accountability--full stop. Otherwise, we fail people again.
And when that happens, voters will look for someone louder, more extreme.
I get laughed at when I say this, but I don't think Donald Trump is the bottom. I think someone worse could come along and take this country down an even darker path.
That's why this moment matters.
Yes, this period has been chaotic and damaging. But it's also an opportunity--to fix what's been broken for decades, to restore dignity, and to build a system that actually lets people live the lives they were promised.
We can do that. I believe we can.
But don't let anyone confuse empathy with weakness. Empathy is strength. It lets you see clearly and act decisively when it matters most.
The best leaders are strong, clear-eyed, and willing to act. We can be compassionate and still hold the line.
If we're serious about fixing this country, we have to be both.

Peter, **The Equality PAC just endorsed our campaign! **This is a powerful statement recognizing Dan’s tireless work defending LGBTQ+ rights. That work is more urgent now than ever. The Supreme Court just overturned Colorado's ban on conversion therapy aimed at young people struggling with their sexual orientation or gender identity, calling that bogus “therapy” free speech. Leading medical groups from the AMA to the American Academy of Pediatrics say conversion therapy is discredited and harmful. But yet again, the Supreme Court used “free speech” to trample over the health and wellness of our children. For families in NY-10 — home to the Stonewall legacy — this is deeply personal. When courts and politicians chip away at protections, it’s the job of Congress to restore them. Dan has been leading the fight for stronger federal protections, pushing for ethics and medical oversight, and demanding that hospitals continue providing gender affirming care to trans children. **Equality PAC called Dan a “fighter,” and they’re right. But endorsements alone won’t change the law.** We need a groundswell of support from our community to show Congress that voters demand action to keep LGBTQ+ youth safe. body:
Allow me to introduce myself to you |
---

Peter,

You may already know who I am from my basketball career. Or, maybe you’re just hearing about me for the first time through my Senate Campaign. Either way, I wanted to formally introduce myself and share my story. [**_Afterward, I’m going to ask you to send a small contribution to my campaign as I continue to fight to Flip Minnesota Red._**](https://links.iterable.com/u/click?_t=ce1ce9e616484205a28a45cfaf96cecf&_m=bb10e7031fd347a0bef4acb4539eeb14&_e=bc8dxR7YIy_CImGJ8vvXsRAK1ksLQE65ZbHxGOu4qTX5nvhyuPZrPWRFtYJQn-NXJBlHYipCi0zmQQjzQlXvW_MpI8wVNESnYFGRCvK-dMRa-DFohYOuc7_xj06xxADc4AHfdMPM_Gwi_VyLkB7ri-ToJJYM0crdrAybiCjYcZK3cL7qRiYhf8BEtApE3sCLfw82xEoHrvyHNKwiEU-sztc5mY0MW2Ht3-2mKU2s35gDtEnR0g9AROaN7ZwXR8SNscWP5kZez6Y21AhjjVgV4KmjBWCgM9EYIfxySh0IrowyH3ULjkUeRDVHy14LWBeJ5mh8BiYQ1_Y9oVf51yW-Cjjq1hosTuzGbx8mEmV0dMjmDJngnYss2mLD_7koomF_vUX0cInaVcJSLRbnbhXttmWBqJseZP5GAv1mcZa-ZKBNtPHO6wwUWTBewbyl1QKgg73q9ymdjfJVgFOV-VtDoBmKY2QskyA3VrYf4sQgPUFpMh3BSHy0Ep7SnBuueUDrbCJnBAXtDhl4rzlD0PChEyrgPBKcOpM77ApeU5K2zJ_8ygGVVdGlGvZg2Dd1D9T_)

I was born and raised in the Twin Cities in Minnesota, mainly in the Rondo Community of St. Paul. At the age of five, I started playing sports, and at nine years old, I was already playing basketball on the Northside of Minneapolis. My mother was a single mother who worked tirelessly to give me a better life. I went to school in Rondo and began to excel at basketball. By 10th grade, I was ranked as a top 20 player in the country. I remember dreaming of reaching the NBA one day– a dream shared by millions of kids.

[](https://links.iterable.com/u/click?_t=ce1ce9e616484205a28a45cfaf96cecf&_m=bb10e7031fd347a0bef4acb4539eeb14&_e=bc8dxR7YIy_CImGJ8vvXsRAK1ksLQE65ZbHxGOu4qTX5nvhyuPZrPWRFtYJQn-NXJBlHYipCi0zmQQjzQlXvW_MpI8wVNESnYFGRCvK-dMRa-DFohYOuc7_xj06xxADc4AHfdMPM_Gwi_VyLkB7ri-ToJJYM0crdrAybiCjYcZK3cL7qRiYhf8BEtApE3sCLDmBPTgIIQjm43tcPvuYlqfb5VxHwzSH9-XBsbXLIDx_sYimHngpn8j8iVQKJV7SWVLahKAETguUrSlq0vf52nmApjvCM-3JZhrtzhYY3HUkI1koEjTGgGoW0Al5wGtGF1ClpIHQSO71yHYz-yEOY8V0B8y6j8oF2DoLFflJxm_tMLVcmRyCfv2YTLCmh8mijwEOUplLsfazuZ98Uj2rhjl2gBHJXuv74jOeGDg9I6B9-Z08HT2PrsieKdPH-oUOC1fCHY0cT3s_M4eIy_8JRyUHfEQLDc609tDQAHXy1iwK63IfmvJiUnEPhDDPscS3PVFUL1BJAgjkmHDH9RhDvbdMxPvpKCP_t33CTPIBjVWyip_sHRsGTXGiBGFehCFyA)
I accepted a scholarship at the University of Minnesota, but shortly after transferred to Iowa State. There, I won multiple basketball awards while working hard in class and being named on the Dean’s List for academics.

[](https://links.iterable.com/u/click?_t=ce1ce9e616484205a28a45cfaf96cecf&_m=bb10e7031fd347a0bef4acb4539eeb14&_e=bc8dxR7YIy_CImGJ8vvXsRAK1ksLQE65ZbHxGOu4qTX5nvhyuPZrPWRFtYJQn-NXJBlHYipCi0zmQQjzQlXvW_MpI8wVNESnYFGRCvK-dMRa-DFohYOuc7_xj06xxADc4AHfdMPM_Gwi_VyLkB7ri-ToJJYM0crdrAybiCjYcZK3cL7qRiYhf8BEtApE3sCL-KEVjzAPxjqe11eq_eubzja_qNTsr8IpNIVxQPWMdg2wo8giOWmnpKvQnYDbaRau8ZO-DFPeY0bXka7eP63x_TsfWLSv88VRlzgR-McdkknBbwDqnNfPlNN7OGzXrnS7j4l95tmYicSxIMqEZCYkf5TLsaZQUDW1TLxDwkpOdZXcENxMFlYiURPod6z36IViof78TsPrcXkg91jv9G8O3xNvr5vSsnVij2dWOOp_cYsgsbBWb4O5bJsxRFcrizfs9hEy3RqHe1h7ZP4KTipm-eOds8H7hbfl_5ELoDAzkNn2Dc6AY1JGIIl3ybdPNLA_GVm1Ozo_Afnef9jDq5qZwt7mZM9Nb-sC1Zdmm8hXdzZoqygvlX80QnYshvjrlvpT)
Finally, my dream came true. I was selected in the first round of the 2012 NBA Draft, going to the Houston Rockets. While playing at the highest level of basketball competition in the world, I began to voice concerns about the NBA’s Collective Bargaining Agreement (CBA), specifically regarding mental health policy, which at the time did not exist.

Eventually, my concerns became a dispute between the NBA and myself, until I demanded that the NBA spearhead the mental health conversation through policy. This led to the end of my NBA career, but my work led to the NBA implementing policies to support players’ mental health.

| | Lifе and death Son of Mykhailo Sulyma, Ivan came from a petty noble (szlachta) family. He was born in Rohoshchi (next to Chernihiv). He served as an estate overseer for Stanisław Żółkiewski and later the family of Daniłowicze who inherited his lands; for that service in 1620 he was awarded three villages: Sulimówka, Kuczakiw and Lebedyn. Аll the villages todаy belong to the Boryspil Raion, Kyiv Oblast. His sons included Stepan (died 1659), a captain of Boryspil company, and Fedir (died 1691), a colonel of Pereiaslav regiment. He became popular among the unregistered Cossacks, leading them on campaigns to plunder Crimea and other Ottoman vassal territories. For organizing a revolt on an Ottoman slave galley and freeing Christian slaves[1] he received a medal from Pope Paul V himself. Eventually, Sulyma reached the rank of the hetman, which he held from 1628 to 1629 and 1630 to 1635. In 1635, after returning from an expedition to Black Sea against the Ottomans, he decided to rebel against the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, which at that time controlled most of the Cossack territories, and whose nobility was trying to turn militant Cossacks into serfs.[citation needed] Ivan Sulyma took part in numerous campaigns of Sagaidachny against Tatars and Turks. In particular, it was the famous capture of Kafa (modern Theodosia), the main center of the slave trade on the Black Sea, Trapezont, Izmail, and also two attacks on Tsaregrad. On the night of 3 to 4 August 1635 he took the newly constructed Kodak fortress by surprise, burning it and executing its crew of about 200 people under Jean Marion. Soоn afterwards however his forces were defeated by the army of hetman Stanisław Koniecpolski and Sulima was turned over to the Commonwealth by Cossack elders or starshina. Together with several other leaders of his rebellion, Hetman Sulyma was executed in Warsaw on 12 December 1635. At first, the Polish King Władysław IV Waza, known for his friendly attitude towards the Cossacks, was hesitant to execute Sulyma, especially since he was a person upon whom the Pope himself bestowed his medal. However, pressured by the nobility who wanted to show that no rebellions against the 'established оrder' would be tolerated, the оrder for an execution was given; after being tortured, Sulyma was cut to pieces and his body parts were hung on the city walls of Warsaw

Egyptian hieroglyphs were the formal writing system used in Ancient Egypt for writing the Egyptian language. Hieroglyphs combined logographic, syllabic and alphabetic elements, with some 1,000 distinct characters.[3][4] Cursive hieroglyphs were used for religious literature on papyrus and wood. The later hieratic and demotic Egyptian scripts were derived from hieroglyphic writing, as was the Proto-Sinaitic script that later evolved into the Phoenician alphabet.[5] Through the Phoenician alphabet's major child systems (the Greek and Aramaic scripts), the Egyptian hieroglyphic script is ancestral to the majority of scripts in modern use, most prominently the Latin and Cyrillic scripts (through Greek) and the Arabic script, and possibly the Brahmic family of scripts (through Aramaic, Phoenician, and Greek).[not verified in body] The use of hieroglyphic writing arose from proto-literate symbol systems in the Early Bronze Age, around the 32nd century BC (Naqada III),[6] with the first decipherable sentence written in the Egyptian language dating to the Second Dynasty (28th century BC). Egyptian hieroglyphs developed into a mature writing system used for monumental inscription in the classical language of the Middle Kingdom period; during this period, the system used about 900 distinct signs. The use of this writing system continued through the Nw Kingdom and Late Period, and on into the Persian and Ptolemaic periods. Late survivals of hieroglyphic use are found well into the Roman period, extending into the 4th century AD.[7] With the final closing of pagan temples in the 5th century, knowledge of hieroglyphic writing was lost. Although attempts were made, the script remained undeciphered throughout the Middle Ages and the early modern period. The decipherment of hieroglyphic writing was finally accomplished in the 1820s by Jean-François Champollion, with the help of the Rosetta Stone.[8] The number of words contained in al Ancient Egyptian (i.e. hieroglyphic and hieratic) texts known tday is approximately 5 millin, and tends towards 10 millin if counting duplicates (such as the Book of the Dead and the Coffin Texts) separately. The most complete compendium of Ancient Egyptian, Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache, contains 1.5–1.7 millin words.[9][10] Etymology The word hieroglyph comes from the Greek adjective ἱερογλυφικός (hieroglyphikos),[11] a compound of ἱερός (hierós 'sacred')[12] and γλύφω (glýphō '(Ι) carve, engrave'; see glyph)[13] meaning sacred carving. Egyptian hieroglyphs were the formal writing system used in Ancient Egypt for writing the Egyptian language. Hieroglyphs combined logographic, syllabic and alphabetic elements, with some 1,000 distinct characters.[3][4] Cursive hieroglyphs were used for religious literature on papyrus and wood. The later hieratic and demotic Egyptian scripts were derived from hieroglyphic writing, as was the Proto-Sinaitic script that later evolved into the Phoenician alphabet.[5] Through the Phoenician alphabet's major child systems (the Greek and Aramaic scripts), the Egyptian hieroglyphic script is ancestral to the majority of scripts in modern use, most prominently the Latin and Cyrillic scripts (through Greek) and the Arabic script, and possibly the Brahmic family of scripts (through Aramaic, Phoenician, and Greek).[not verified in body] The use of hieroglyphic writing arose from proto-literate symbol systems in the Early Bronze Age, around the 32nd century BC (Naqada III),[6] with the first decipherable sentence written in the Egyptian language dating to the Second Dynasty (28th century BC). Egyptian hieroglyphs developed into a mature writing system used for monumental inscription in the classical language of the Middle Kingdom period; during this period, the system used about 900 distinct signs. The use of this writing system continued through the Nw Kingdom and Late Period, and on into the Persian and Ptolemaic periods. Late survivals of hieroglyphic use are found well into the Roman period, extending into the 4th century AD.[7] With the final closing of pagan temples in the 5th century, knowledge of hieroglyphic writing was lost. Although attempts were made, the script remained undeciphered throughout the Middle Ages and the early modern period. The decipherment of hieroglyphic writing was finally accomplished in the 1820s by Jean-François Champollion, with the help of the Rosetta Stone.[8] The number of words contained in al Ancient Egyptian (i.e. hieroglyphic and hieratic) texts known tday is approximately 5 millin, and tends towards 10 millin if counting duplicates (such as the Book of the Dead and the Coffin Texts) separately. The most complete compendium of Ancient Egyptian, Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache, contains 1.5–1.7 millin words.[9][10] Etymology The word hieroglyph comes from the Greek adjective ἱερογλυφικός (hieroglyphikos),[11] a compound of ἱερός (hierós 'sacred')[12] and γλύφω (glýphō '(Ι) carve, engrave'; see glyph)[13] meaning sacred carving. The glyphs themselves, since the Ptolemaic period, were called τὰ ἱερογλυφικὰ [γράμματα] (tà hieroglyphikà [grámmata]) "the sacred engraved letters", the Greek counterpart to the Egyptian expression of mdw.w-nṯr "god's words".[14] Greek ἱερόγλυφος meant "a carver of hieroglyphs".[15] In English, hieroglyph as a noun is recorded from 1590, originally short for nominalized hieroglyphic (1580s, with a plural hieroglyphics), from adjectival use (hieroglyphic character).[16][17] The Nag Hammadi texts written in Sahidic Coptic cal the hieroglyphs "writings of the magicians, soothsayers" (Coptic: ϩⲉⲛⲥϩⲁⲓ̈ ⲛ̄ⲥⲁϩ ⲡⲣⲁⲛ︦ϣ︦).[18]
